title: Strong in Grace, Straight with Truth
summary: Paul charges Timothy to endure as Christ’s soldier, guard and pass on the gospel, handle the word rightly, and correct opponents with patient gentleness.
historicalContext: Paul writes from a Roman prison, chained like a criminal and expecting death, while defections in Asia have left him isolated (1:15). Timothy, still in Ephesus, faces a congregation unsettled by teachers whose speculative word-battles were spreading through the church. Two of them are named: Hymenaeus, already disciplined earlier (1 Timothy 1:20), and Philetus, who taught that the resurrection had already taken place, probably by turning the hope of a bodily rising into a purely inward experience. The apostolic generation was nearing its end. Paul therefore thinks beyond his own lifetime, urging Timothy to entrust the gospel to reliable teachers who can carry it forward. Military service, athletic games, and farm labor, all familiar to the Greco-Roman world, supply the pictures by which he explains the cost and reward of ministry under pressure.
literaryContext: Chapter 2 turns the personal appeal of chapter 1 into a set of concrete charges. “Thou therefore” links Timothy to the faithfulness of Onesiphorus and sets him against those who turned away. The first half (vv. 1–13) presses the call to share suffering, using three images and grounding them in the risen Christ, Paul’s own chains, and a trustworthy saying about dying, enduring, and reigning with Christ. The second half (vv. 14–26) moves to the false teaching, contrasting the straight handling of “the word of truth” with gangrenous talk, God’s firm foundation with overturned faith, honorable vessels with dishonorable ones, and the gentle servant of the Lord with quarrelsome disputers. The chapter prepares for the description of the last days in chapter 3 and the final charge of chapter 4.
themes: Strength drawn from the grace that is in Christ
Faithful transmission of the apostolic gospel
Endurance that shares in Christ’s sufferings and reign
Handling the word of truth with integrity
The future bodily resurrection against spiritualized error
Holiness and gentleness in the Lord’s servant

outline.title: Strengthened to Serve and Endure
outline.summary: Timothy is to draw strength from Christ’s grace, entrust the gospel to faithful teachers, and learn single-minded endurance from the soldier, athlete, and farmer.

outline.title: Remembering the Risen Christ
outline.summary: The resurrection of David’s Son, Paul’s chains for the elect, and a trustworthy saying about union with Christ ground the call to endure.

outline.title: The Word Rightly Handled
outline.summary: Timothy must refuse word-battles, handle the truth straight, and resist teaching that denied the coming resurrection, resting on God’s sure foundation.

outline.title: Vessels Fit for the Master
outline.summary: Those who cleanse themselves from dishonorable ways become sanctified, useful vessels who flee youthful desires and pursue righteousness with the pure in heart.

outline.title: The Lord’s Servant and His Opponents
outline.summary: Avoiding foolish disputes, the servant of the Lord corrects opponents with gentleness, hoping God will grant repentance and release from the devil’s snare.

verses.bibleText: Thou therefore, my son, be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The word “therefore” ties this charge to the scene Paul has just painted. All in Asia have turned away, Phygellus and Hermogenes among them, while Onesiphorus searched Rome until he found the prisoner and was unashamed of his chain. Timothy must now choose which example he will follow. The emphatic “thou” singles him out from the deserters, and the tender address “my son” reminds him that the appeal comes from a spiritual father who has known him since Lystra.

The command is to “be strong,” yet the Greek form is passive and continuous. Timothy is told to keep on being strengthened. Paul does not ask him to summon courage from his own temperament, which seems to have been sensitive and prone to tears. Strength is something received, day after day, from a source outside himself. The same verb describes the Lord standing with Paul at his trial and strengthening him (4:17), and it appears in the call to be strong in the Lord and in the power of his might.

That source is “the grace that is in Christ Jesus.” Grace here is God’s undeserved favor, and that favor carries with it the power to serve and to suffer. The phrase locates the grace in Christ himself; it belongs to those who are united to him and is available to every believer, not only to apostles. Earlier Paul spoke of grace given in Christ before the world began (1:9). The same grace that called Timothy now sustains him.

Everything Paul will ask in this chapter—hardship, discipline, toil, study, purity, and patient correction—rests on this opening line. Duties that would crush a person relying on natural resolve become possible for one who keeps drawing on Christ. The minister’s first task is to remain a receiver.

wordNotes.explanation: A present passive imperative, best understood as “keep on being made strong.” The verb consistently describes spiritual empowerment that God or Christ supplies. Timothy’s part is ongoing dependence, while the strength itself comes from the Lord who empowers his servants for witness and endurance.

wordNotes.term: ἐν τῇ χάριτι τῇ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ (en tē chariti tē en Christō Iēsou) — in the grace that is in Christ Jesus
wordNotes.explanation: The repeated article ties the grace closely to Christ. Grace is God’s unmerited favor, and in Paul it includes the enabling power that flows from that favor. It is found only in union with Christ and is therefore shared by all who belong to him.

verses.bibleText: And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Personal strength is joined at once to a public responsibility. What Timothy has received he must hand on. “The things that thou hast heard of me” covers the whole body of apostolic teaching, the “form of sound words” Paul urged him to hold fast (1:13). This message came largely through spoken preaching and instruction, and Timothy had heard it over many years of travel and shared labor.

“Among many witnesses” most naturally means that Paul’s teaching was never a private or secret doctrine. It was proclaimed openly in synagogues, households, and congregations, and many fellow workers and believers could confirm its content. Some have connected the phrase with Timothy’s ordination, when elders laid hands on him, and that occasion may be included. The wider point is that the gospel Timothy carries can be checked against public testimony. Error often thrives on hidden knowledge; the apostolic message stands in the light.

Timothy must “commit” these things, a word used for depositing something valuable with a trustworthy keeper. Paul had already described the gospel as a good deposit entrusted to Timothy (1:14). Now the deposit is to pass to “faithful men,” people whose reliability has been proved and who can be trusted not to lose, neglect, or alter what they receive. They must also be “able to teach others also.” Two qualifications appear: fidelity to the truth and competence to communicate it.

The verse sketches four links in a chain: Paul, Timothy, faithful teachers, and others beyond them. Paul knew his own voice would soon be silenced. He does not secure the future by appointing an infallible office or a secret tradition. He secures it by the careful teaching of the same message to dependable people, who are measured always by the apostolic word now preserved in Scripture.

Every congregation shares this concern. Leaders who do not train others leave the church vulnerable when they are gone. Faithful ministry looks past itself and invests in those who will keep the truth after us.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to entrust something to another for safekeeping, as a deposit is placed in reliable hands. It echoes the language of the “good thing” committed to Timothy. The gospel is treated as a treasure to be guarded and passed on intact.

Here pistos stresses trustworthiness rather than simply being a believer, which is assumed. The people chosen must be dependable stewards of the message, tested in loyalty to the truth and able to teach it competently to others.

verses.bibleText: Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul returns to the call he first issued in 1:8. The best-supported Greek reading is a compound verb meaning “suffer hardship with” someone, so that Timothy is invited to take his share of suffering alongside Paul. The KJV “endure hardness” captures the grit of the command, while the compound adds fellowship: Timothy will not suffer alone, for the apostle in chains is already in the line ahead of him.

The comparison is with “a good soldier of Jesus Christ.” Soldiers expected rough conditions, long marches, short rations, and danger. Hardship belonged to the job. Paul often used military pictures for the Christian life and called co-workers like Epaphroditus and Archippus his fellow soldiers. The adjective “good” marks a soldier who is excellent and praiseworthy in service, and the genitive shows whose army he belongs to. Christ enlisted Timothy, and Christ is the one he serves.

The call implies that suffering is part of ordinary Christian witness, not a sign that something has gone wrong. In the great controversy between Christ and Satan, faithful servants will face opposition, as Paul will say plainly in 3:12. Timothy was perhaps of gentle disposition, yet gentleness of manner and toughness under pressure can belong to the same person when both are rooted in loyalty to the Captain.

wordNotes.explanation: The preferred reading combines “with” and “suffer evil,” yielding “take your share of suffering.” The prefix implies partnership with Paul and with all who suffer for the gospel, so that hardship becomes a shared calling within the fellowship of Christ’s servants.

verses.bibleText: No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life; that he may please him who hath chosen him to be a soldier.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
A general principle of military life explains the soldier image. “No man that warreth” describes someone on active duty, engaged in a campaign. Such a person does not let himself become entangled “with the affairs of this life.” The verb pictures being caught or wrapped up in something, as a cloak might tangle a man’s weapons. Civilian business, trade, and private projects are not evil in themselves; the problem comes when they wind around the soldier so that he can no longer respond to orders.

The purpose clause supplies the motive: “that he may please him who hath chosen him to be a soldier.” The commander enlisted him. His time, energy, and loyalty therefore belong first to that commander. A soldier who divides his attention between the campaign and his own enterprises will serve poorly and may endanger others.

The application to Timothy is by analogy. Paul does not forbid every kind of ordinary work. He himself made tents, and he defended his right to do so as a way of advancing the gospel without burdening others. Elsewhere he argued that churches should support those who labor in the word so that they can give themselves to it. The point concerns priority and focus. Earthly duties must serve the great aim of pleasing Christ and must never crowd it out.

Jesus warned that the cares, riches, and pleasures of this life can choke the word until it brings no fruit. The minister and every believer face the same danger. Possessions, ambitions, entertainments, and anxieties can multiply until the soul is tangled. The soldier of Christ regularly asks whether present commitments help or hinder obedience to the One who called him. The desire to please human audiences also entangles, and Paul refuses it; the approval that matters comes from the Lord who enlisted us.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to be woven into or caught up in something, used figuratively for involvement that restricts freedom. Peter uses it of those again entangled in the world’s defilements. Here it describes affairs that bind a soldier so that he cannot serve freely.

wordNotes.term: τῷ στρατολογήσαντι (tō stratologēsanti) — him who hath chosen him to be a soldier
wordNotes.explanation: The participle describes the officer who enlisted or recruited the soldier. A soldier serves because someone called him into service. Timothy belongs to Christ, who chose him, and pleasing that Commander governs everything else.

verses.bibleText: And if a man also strive for masteries, yet is he not crowned, except he strive lawfully.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The second picture comes from the athletic games. To “strive for masteries” translates a verb meaning to compete in a contest, the word from which “athlete” comes. Readers in Asia Minor knew the great festivals, the crowds, the training regimens, and the victor’s wreath of leaves.

Yet a competitor “is not crowned, except he strive lawfully.” An athlete who broke the rules was disqualified, however fast he ran. Some games required contestants to swear they had completed months of training before they could enter. Victory belonged only to those who submitted to the discipline and regulations of the event.

Paul leaves Timothy to draw the lesson. The Christian contest has its own rules, set by the life and teaching of Christ. Faithfulness to sound doctrine, a life consistent with the message, and willingness to suffer hardship all belong to these rules. A ministry may be busy and impressive, yet if it abandons the truth or contradicts the character of Christ, it will receive no crown. Jesus warned of those who will cite their mighty works on the last day and still be disowned.

The analogy also differs from the stadium in one encouraging way. At the games only one runner took the prize. In Christ’s contest every faithful competitor will be crowned. Paul later speaks of a crown of righteousness laid up for him and for all who love Christ’s appearing (4:8). That crown is given “at that day,” when the Lord returns, and it does not wither like the wreaths of the games.

wordNotes.explanation: The adverb means “according to the rules” of the contest and stands emphatically in the sentence. Paul uses the same word of using the law lawfully. In the Christian race the rules are those God has set, including faithfulness to his truth and readiness to suffer for it.

The verb refers to receiving the victor’s wreath. Earthly wreaths perished quickly, which makes them a fitting contrast to the imperishable crown God promises his faithful servants at the appearing of Christ.

verses.bibleText: The husbandman that laboureth must be first partaker of the fruits.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The third picture is the farmer. The emphasis falls on the participle “that laboureth,” the farmer who works hard, toils, and wearies himself. Plowing, sowing, weeding, and harvesting demanded long days of exhausting effort. Paul uses the same word family for his own strenuous labor in the gospel and for elders who labor in word and doctrine.

Such a farmer “must be first partaker of the fruits.” It is fitting that the one who toiled should share in the harvest. Some have read this as a reminder of the minister’s right to material support, a theme Paul develops in 1 Corinthians 9. Others see a reference to the joy of seeing converts and growth. The simplest reading is that the image itself assures reward: hard work in the field is followed by a share in the crop. Timothy should expect that faithful labor for Christ will not go unrewarded.

There is also a practical lesson. A farmer feeds himself from what he grows before he can feed others. The minister must himself be nourished by the truth he sows and display its fruit in his own character. Laziness forfeits the harvest, and so does a teacher who handles the word for others without ever eating it.

wordNotes.term: τὸν κοπιῶντα γεωργόν (ton kopiōnta geōrgon) — the husbandman that laboureth
wordNotes.explanation: Geōrgos is a tiller of the soil, and kopiaō means to toil to the point of weariness. Paul frequently uses kopiaō for the exhausting labor of gospel ministry, which he attributes finally to God’s grace working in him.

verses.bibleText: Consider what I say; and the Lord give thee understanding in all things.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Having offered three pictures without spelling out every application, Paul tells Timothy to “consider” them. The verb asks for careful thought, turning the images over until their meaning is grasped. Paul treats Timothy as a mature worker able to draw out the lessons for himself: single-minded loyalty from the soldier, disciplined faithfulness from the athlete, persevering toil from the farmer.

The promise follows: “the Lord give thee understanding in all things.” The better-attested reading has a future, “the Lord will give.” Human reflection and divine illumination work together. Timothy must think, and the Lord grants insight. Wisdom literature had long taught that the Lord gives wisdom and understanding, and Paul prayed that believers might be filled with spiritual understanding. No minister can master his calling by memorized rules alone. New situations arise for which no direct precedent exists, and the faithful servant brings them to God, expecting light as he studies and obeys.

wordNotes.explanation: A present imperative calling for continued reflection and comprehension. Timothy is to think through what Paul has said until he understands its implications for his own ministry.
The noun denotes insight that grasps how things fit together. In Paul it is a gift that God supplies to those who seek to know his will, and it grows as believers ponder and practice the truth.

verses.bibleText: Remember that Jesus Christ of the seed of David was raised from the dead according to my gospel:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
After three illustrations from ordinary life, Paul points Timothy to the supreme example. “Remember that Jesus Christ … was raised” may be rendered more directly, “Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead.” The present imperative calls for continual remembrance. Timothy is to keep Christ himself before his mind, especially when hardship tempts him to shrink back.

Two descriptions fill out the name. First, he is “raised from the dead.” The Greek perfect participle stresses a lasting result: Jesus was raised and remains the living, risen Lord. The one who suffered and was placed among the dead now stands beyond death’s reach, the firstfruits of all who will rise. For a man in chains facing execution, and for a younger colleague called to share his suffering, nothing could be more steadying. The path of faithfulness passed through the cross for Jesus too, and it ended in resurrection. The empty tomb is God’s public vindication of his Son and the guarantee of his people’s future.

Second, he is “of the seed of David.” The phrase roots Jesus firmly in history and in the promises of the Old Testament. God had sworn that a descendant of David would sit on his throne forever. Jesus is that promised King, truly human, born into a real family line, and yet raised to an endless reign. Paul joins the same two truths in the opening of Romans, where Christ is David’s seed according to the flesh and declared Son of God with power by the resurrection. If any at Ephesus were tempted to treat the Savior as a spiritual idea detached from flesh and history, this confession answered them.

“According to my gospel” does not imply a private message. Paul means the gospel entrusted to him and preached by him, the same good news proclaimed by all the apostles. Its center is a person: the human, Davidic Messiah who died and rose. Christian ministry draws its courage from this living Lord, and every sermon worth hearing returns to him.

wordNotes.explanation: A present imperative meaning “keep in mind” or “continually call to mind.” Biblical remembering is more than recalling a fact; it is holding a truth before the heart so that it shapes conduct and confidence under trial.

wordNotes.term: ἐγηγερμένον ἐκ νεκρῶν (egēgermenon ek nekrōn) — raised from the dead
wordNotes.explanation: The perfect passive participle describes Christ as one who was raised and continues in risen life. “From the dead” places him once among those who had died. The passive implies God’s action in raising him.

verses.bibleText: Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The gospel Paul has just summarized is the very cause of his present suffering. “Wherein I suffer trouble” refers to the sphere of that gospel: because he preached the risen Son of David, he now endures evil treatment. The verb is the same one used in the call for Timothy to share hardship, so Paul’s own situation becomes the living illustration of his appeal.

He suffers “as an evil doer, even unto bonds.” The word for “evil doer” was used of serious criminals; Luke uses it of the two men crucified beside Jesus. Under Nero, Christians were slandered as wrongdoers and enemies of society. Paul, a Roman citizen and an apostle of peace, is treated like a felon and kept in chains. The disgrace was part of the suffering. Yet his experience mirrors his Lord’s, who was numbered with the transgressors.

Then comes the triumphant contrast: “but the word of God is not bound.” A man can be chained; the message cannot. Paul plays on the language of binding. During his first Roman imprisonment the gospel had reached the palace guard and members of Caesar’s household. Now, though his own movements are restricted, Timothy, Titus, Luke, and many others carry the word into new regions. God’s purposes do not depend on the freedom of any one servant.

The history of the church has repeated this pattern. Rulers have imprisoned preachers, banned translations, and burned Bibles, yet the word has continued to run. A believer who feels silenced by circumstances can take heart: the power lies in the message, not in the messenger’s liberty.

wordNotes.explanation: The term denotes a criminal guilty of grave misdeeds. Its only other New Testament use describes the men crucified with Jesus. Paul feels the shame of being classed with such offenders for the sake of the gospel.

wordNotes.term: οὐ δέδεται (ou dedetai) — is not bound
wordNotes.explanation: The perfect tense affirms that God’s word has not been chained and remains unchained. The verb deliberately echoes Paul’s “bonds,” setting the imprisoned apostle beside the free and advancing message.

verses.bibleText: Therefore I endure all things for the elect's sakes, that they may also obtain the salvation which is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Therefore” draws a conclusion from the unbound word. Since God’s message keeps advancing, Paul’s chains are not wasted. He “endure[s] all things for the elect’s sakes.” The verb shifts from suffering evil to steadfast endurance, the posture of one who stays at his post under pressure instead of fleeing. The same verb appears in the faithful saying that follows (v. 12), so Paul’s personal endurance anticipates the endurance required of every believer.

The elect are those whom God has chosen in Christ and is drawing to himself through the gospel. Paul labors and suffers so that they too, alongside him, “may also obtain the salvation which is in Christ Jesus.” God’s choice does not make preaching unnecessary. The chosen are reached through faithful witnesses, and Paul counts his sufferings worthwhile if they serve that purpose. Election in Scripture is always in Christ, and it calls forth earnest mission rather than passivity.

The salvation is “in Christ Jesus,” found only in union with him, and it comes “with eternal glory.” Salvation begins now in forgiveness and new life, and it reaches its fulfillment when Christ appears and his people share his glory. Paul contrasts the brief affliction of the present with that lasting splendor. Chains, disgrace, and death look different when weighed against glory that has no end.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb describes remaining steadfast under trial instead of running away. Paul uses it absolutely with “all things,” indicating a settled readiness to bear whatever the gospel ministry brings for the sake of others.

wordNotes.term: μετὰ δόξης αἰωνίου (meta doxēs aiōniou) — with eternal glory
wordNotes.explanation: Glory is the radiant presence and splendor of God. The redeemed will share it fully at Christ’s appearing. Paul sets this enduring glory against the temporary pressures of present suffering.

verses.bibleText: It is a faithful saying: For if we be dead with him, we shall also live with him:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“It is a faithful saying” introduces the last of five such sayings in the Pastoral Letters. The formula marks a well-known statement that the church recognized as trustworthy, and Paul endorses it. The rhythmic, balanced lines of verses 11–13 suggest that it may have been sung or recited, perhaps in connection with baptism. Each line begins with “if” and pairs what “we” do with what Christ does.

The first line reads: “For if we be dead with him, we shall also live with him.” The verb “be dead with” is a past tense, pointing to a completed event. Some have taken it as martyrdom, but the New Testament never speaks of martyrdom as dying “with” Christ in this way, and a martyr’s death would not normally precede the call to endure in the next line. The closest parallel is Romans 6, where Paul says that believers were buried with Christ by baptism into death and that if we died with Christ we shall also live with him. The death in view is the believer’s union with Christ in his death: the old self crucified, the reign of sin broken, the person who once lived for self brought to an end. Baptism is the public sign of this death and new beginning.

“We shall also live with him” follows from that union. Those who share his death share his life. In Romans 6 this life is first a present walk in newness of life, lived to God. It also stretches forward to the resurrection, when believers who sleep in the dust will be raised to an endless life with their Lord. Present spiritual life and future bodily life are two stages of one gift.

The saying fits Paul’s situation precisely. A prisoner facing execution and a younger minister called to suffer both need assurance that death does not have the last word. Those who have already died with Christ to sin need not fear dying for him in the body, for life with him is promised and secured by his own resurrection.

wordNotes.term: πιστὸς ὁ λόγος (pistos ho logos) — it is a faithful saying
wordNotes.explanation: A formula found five times in the Pastoral Letters, marking a statement the church accepted as reliable. It both introduces and commends what follows, here a rhythmic four-line saying about union with Christ.

wordNotes.term: συναπεθάνομεν (synapethanomen) — we be dead with him
wordNotes.explanation: An aorist verb with the prefix “with,” meaning “we died together with.” In Paul’s usage it describes the believer’s participation in Christ’s death, signified in baptism, through which the old life of sin is ended.

verses.bibleText: If we suffer, we shall also reign with him: if we deny him, he also will deny us:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The second line moves from the past to the present: “If we suffer, we shall also reign with him.” The Greek verb is the same one translated “endure” in verse 10. It means to keep enduring, to remain loyal under hardship, rejection, and persecution. The present tense describes a continuing posture rather than a single crisis. The life begun by dying with Christ is lived out in steadfast endurance.

The promise is that those who endure “shall also reign with him.” Jesus told his disciples that those who continued with him in his trials would sit on thrones. Daniel saw the kingdom given to the saints of the Most High. Revelation pictures the redeemed reigning with Christ during the thousand years and then forever in the restored earth. This reign belongs to the future, after the time of enduring has ended. Paul once rebuked Corinthian believers who acted as if they were already reigning; the present is the season of endurance, and the reign comes at Christ’s return.

Then the saying turns sharply from encouragement to warning: “if we deny him, he also will deny us.” The words echo Jesus’ own: whoever denies me before men, I will deny before my Father in heaven. To deny Christ is to disown a person one has professed to know. It can take the form of open repudiation, silence when loyalty is required, or a life whose deeds contradict its confession. The consequence is reciprocal. Christ will disown the one who disowned him when he comes in glory and the final verdict is spoken.

The warning is meant seriously. A profession of faith is not a guarantee that can be cashed in while a person persists in rejecting the Lord. Yet the next line will show that the saying is aimed at stiffening resolve, not at driving the frail to despair. Peter denied Jesus three times and was restored, because he repented and returned. The denial that brings final denial is a settled refusal of Christ.

wordNotes.term: συμβασιλεύσομεν (symbasileusomen) — we shall reign with him
wordNotes.explanation: A future verb meaning “we shall reign together with.” Its only other New Testament use is Paul’s ironic word to the Corinthians who acted as if already reigning. Sharing Christ’s rule belongs to the age to come.

The verb means to say no to, disown, or repudiate someone with whom there was a prior relationship. It appears in Jesus’ warning about denial and in Peter’s denials. Denial may be verbal or shown by conduct that contradicts profession.

verses.bibleText: If we believe not, yet he abideth faithful: he cannot deny himself.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The fourth line breaks the expected pattern. After “if we deny him, he also will deny us,” one might expect “if we are faithless, he will be faithless to us.” Instead the saying declares, “If we believe not, yet he abideth faithful: he cannot deny himself.” The first three lines describe a response that matches the human condition. This one describes a response grounded entirely in Christ’s own character.

The verb rendered “believe not” can mean either unbelief or unfaithfulness. Because it is answered by Christ’s faithfulness, the contrast points to unfaithfulness: moments when believers falter, fail to trust, or prove untrue in their loyalty. Such lapses differ from the settled denial of the previous line. The disciples forsook Jesus and fled, and Peter denied him with oaths, yet the risen Lord sought them out, prayed for Peter’s faith, and restored him by the lake. Christ’s faithfulness held when theirs collapsed.

“He abideth faithful” means that he remains what he has always been. His faithfulness is fidelity to his own word and promises. He has promised to receive all who come to him, to forgive those who confess, and to keep those whom the Father has given him. Human wavering cannot overturn those promises.

The closing reason anchors everything: “he cannot deny himself.” God cannot lie; he cannot become untrue to his own nature. This cuts in two directions. It assures the trembling believer that Christ will not abandon his promise to those who turn back to him. It also means that he will not pretend that persistent denial is loyalty, for that too would contradict his holy character. His faithfulness is both the believer’s security and the reason his warnings must be taken seriously.

The line offers no license to sin. It is a refuge for a troubled conscience. A servant like Timothy, aware of his own weakness and of the pressures ahead, could rest not on the strength of his commitment but on the unchanging faithfulness of his Lord. The whole saying ends where all Christian endurance must end: with Christ, who is true even when we are not.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb can denote unbelief or unfaithfulness. Set against Christ’s remaining faithful, it most likely describes the lapses of believers who prove untrue in some measure, as distinct from the settled disowning of Christ in the previous line.

wordNotes.term: ἀρνήσασθαι ἑαυτὸν οὐ δύναται (arnēsasthai heauton ou dynatai) — he cannot deny himself
wordNotes.explanation: To deny himself would be to act contrary to his own being. Christ’s faithfulness flows from his unchanging nature, just as God cannot lie. His promises therefore stand firm, and so does his holiness.

verses.bibleText: Of these things put them in remembrance, charging them before the Lord that they strive not about words to no profit, but to the subverting of the hearers.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The second half of the chapter turns toward the false teaching at Ephesus. “Of these things put them in remembrance” refers to the truths just laid out: strength in grace, endurance, the risen Christ, and the faithful saying. “Them” probably means first the faithful teachers of verse 2, and through them the whole congregation. Timothy is to keep reminding them, for believers forget, and forgotten truth leaves room for novelty.

The reminder comes with a solemn charge “before the Lord.” Teachers are accountable to God, who hears every word spoken in his name. Paul forbids them to “strive … about words.” The term describes word-battles, contentious debates over terms and phrases that turn the faith into a contest of cleverness. Such disputes are “to no profit”: nothing useful comes from them. Worse, they lead “to the subverting of the hearers.” The word gives us “catastrophe” and means overturning or ruin, the opposite of building up.

Paul is not dismissing careful study of language; he will urge exact handling of the word in the next verse. The concern is debate that magnifies trivia, feeds pride, and leaves listeners confused and unsettled. The test of teaching is whether it builds faith, love, and likeness to Christ in those who hear.

wordNotes.explanation: A compound of “word” and “fight,” meaning to wage battles over words. Paul uses the related noun for the morbid craving for controversy that marks false teachers, producing envy, strife, and suspicion instead of godliness.
Literally an overturning or upsetting, used of ruin. Profitless controversy overturns the faith of listeners, the reverse of the edification that true teaching produces.

verses.bibleText: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Having charged others, Timothy must take himself in hand. The best answer to empty word-battles is a teacher whose own handling of Scripture is sound. “Study” in older English meant to be diligent or zealous; the Greek verb conveys eager effort and persistent zeal. It certainly includes careful reading of Scripture, but its scope is wider. Timothy is to spare no effort in his whole ministry.

The aim is “to shew thyself approved unto God.” The verb means to present oneself before someone, and the one who examines is God. Paul lifts the question of approval out of human hands. False teachers sought applause; the faithful worker seeks the verdict of the One whose judgment is never mistaken. “Approved” describes something that has been tested and found genuine, like a coin or metal that passes inspection.

The image becomes that of “a workman that needeth not to be ashamed.” Paul knew manual labor as a tentmaker. A craftsman whose seams are crooked or whose stitching fails feels shame when his work is examined. Ministers are laborers in God’s field, and their work too will be inspected. The workman who need not be ashamed is the one who handles his material properly.

That material is “the word of truth,” and the faithful worker is to be “rightly dividing” it. The verb literally means cutting straight. It was used in the Greek Old Testament of God making the paths of the upright straight. The picture may be of a road cut straight through rough country, a furrow plowed true, or a stone squared to fit. Over time the word came to stress the “straight” rather than the “cutting,” so that it means to handle correctly. Timothy is to treat God’s word in accordance with its intention, letting each part speak in harmony with the whole, giving central truths their proper weight, and keeping secondary matters in their place.

The phrase does not authorize slicing Scripture into separated ages whose commands no longer bind later believers. Its point is integrity. A straight cut leaves no room for twisting texts to fit a theory, building doctrines on isolated phrases, or turning plain statements into allegory. Paul calls the gospel itself “the word of truth” in other letters. The faithful teacher keeps the gospel at the center and lets the whole Bible interpret its parts. Every believer who opens Scripture shares this responsibility. Diligence, honesty before God, and a willingness to be corrected by the text mark those who handle it straight.

wordNotes.explanation: An imperative meaning “be diligent,” “make every effort,” or “be eager.” The KJV’s “study” carried that sense in its day. Paul uses the same verb when urging Timothy to come to him quickly, showing the earnestness involved.

Literally “cutting straight.” In the Greek Old Testament the verb describes straight paths for the upright. Applied to Scripture, it means handling the word correctly and accurately, without distortion, in contrast to those who twist or corrupt it.

verses.bibleText: But shun profane and vain babblings: for they will increase unto more ungodliness.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The positive charge is followed by a negative one: “But shun profane and vain babblings.” The verb means to turn around in order to avoid, to step aside from. Timothy is to keep his distance from talk that is profane, meaning worldly and empty of God, and vain, meaning hollow sound with no substance. Paul used the same description in 1 Timothy 6:20, showing that the same kind of teaching was still troubling Ephesus.

The reason is its trajectory: “they will increase unto more ungodliness.” The verb means to advance or make progress. These teachers may well have thought of themselves as progressive thinkers moving beyond the simple gospel. Paul turns their claim around. They are advancing, yes, but deeper into ungodliness. Empty speculation never stays empty. It draws teachers and listeners alike further from reverence for God and from holy living. Error and moral decline travel together, and a congregation that entertains the one will soon feel the other.

wordNotes.explanation: Literally “empty sounds,” talk that has noise without content. Joined with “profane,” it describes religious chatter that lacks the holiness and substance of God’s truth.
The verb means to make progress or advance. In the Pastoral Letters it is used ironically of advancing in evil, as with deceivers who grow worse and worse. Their supposed progress is a descent.

verses.bibleText: And their word will eat as doth a canker: of whom is Hymenaeus and Philetus;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul adds a second reason to avoid such talk. “Their word will eat as doth a canker.” The KJV “canker” renders the Greek word for gangrene, the spreading death of tissue that moves outward from a wound and consumes healthy flesh. The phrase “will eat” is literally “will have pasture,” a medical expression for an ulcer spreading as cattle graze across a field. False teaching, Paul warns, is not a harmless curiosity confined to a few. It spreads through the body of the church, destroying what was living.

The image carries an implied remedy. Gangrene cannot be tolerated or reasoned with; it must be dealt with decisively before it reaches vital organs. Timothy must not give such talk a platform or a hearing in the congregation.

Paul then names names: “of whom is Hymenaeus and Philetus.” Hymenaeus appeared earlier, with Alexander, as one who had made shipwreck of the faith and been delivered to Satan so that he might learn not to blaspheme (1 Timothy 1:20). Evidently discipline had not ended his influence. Philetus is otherwise unknown. Naming them was not gossip. Timothy and the church needed to recognize the specific voices spreading error so that they could guard themselves. It is a sobering thing to be remembered in Scripture only as a spreader of decay.

wordNotes.explanation: A medical term for gangrene, the spreading decay of flesh. Combined with the expression “will have pasture,” it pictures false teaching consuming the health of the church little by little until the whole body is endangered.

verses.bibleText: Who concerning the truth have erred, saying that the resurrection is past already; and overthrow the faith of some.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul now identifies the specific error. Hymenaeus and Philetus “concerning the truth have erred.” The verb means to miss the mark or swerve from the right path; Paul used it of those who had turned aside from love and faith to vain talk (1 Timothy 1:6). The truth they missed is the gospel itself, “the word of truth” Timothy must handle straight.

Their teaching was “that the resurrection is past already.” In Paul’s letters “the resurrection,” when it refers to believers, means the future event at the coming of Christ when the dead are raised bodily. These teachers claimed that it had already happened. Most likely they spiritualized it, making resurrection a purely inward experience, perhaps the new life received at conversion or baptism. Paul had indeed taught that believers are raised with Christ to walk in newness of life. Twisted out of context, such language could be made to say that there is no further resurrection to wait for. Such a view usually travels with a low estimate of the body and of the created world, an outlook that also fed the ascetic demands mentioned in 1 Timothy 4.

Scripture keeps the hope future and bodily. Christ rose with a real body, the firstfruits of a harvest still to come. The dead in Christ do not rise at the moment of death; they sleep in the grave until the Lord descends from heaven with a shout, and then they rise first. At the last trumpet the dead are raised incorruptible, and mortal bodies put on immortality. Jesus himself said that the hour is coming when all who are in the graves will hear his voice and come forth. Nothing in this teaching locates the believer’s hope in a soul already living on elsewhere. The hope of the dead rests entirely on Christ’s return and his power to raise them.

That is why the error “overthrow[s] the faith of some.” The verb pictures overturning, as Jesus overturned the tables in the temple. If the resurrection is already past, then the grave is final for those who have died, Christ’s coming has lost its purpose, and present suffering has no future vindication. Paul argued at Corinth that denying the resurrection of the dead strikes at Christ’s own resurrection and leaves believers still in their sins. Hope for the future and faith in the present stand or fall together.

The passage warns the church that small reinterpretations of a central doctrine can unravel a whole faith. The resurrection does not lie behind us. It lies ahead, at the appearing of Jesus Christ, and it is certain because he lives.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to miss the target or swerve from the course. It appears three times in the Pastoral Letters, always of those who have deviated from the truth or from faith, marking a departure from the apostolic path.

wordNotes.term: τὴν ἀνάστασιν ἤδη γεγονέναι (tēn anastasin ēdē gegonenai) — the resurrection is past already
wordNotes.explanation: “The resurrection” refers to the expected rising of the dead. The perfect infinitive with “already” claims it has occurred and is complete. Scripture instead places the bodily resurrection of believers at the return of Christ.

verses.bibleText: Nevertheless the foundation of God standeth sure, having this seal, The Lord knoweth them that are his. And, Let every one that nameth the name of Christ depart from iniquity.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Nevertheless” turns the page decisively. Timothy has heard of desertion in Asia, of Paul’s chains, of gangrenous teaching, and of believers whose faith has been overturned. He might wonder whether the whole church is crumbling. Paul answers with confidence: “the foundation of God standeth sure.” Whatever else falls, what God has laid stands firm. The foundation probably refers to the church God has built, the household of God described in 1 Timothy 3:15 as the pillar and ground of the truth. It is founded on Christ and on the apostolic gospel. Its stability does not depend on the faithfulness of every member or leader. It rests on God, who laid it and owns it. The adjective “sure” means solid or immovable, and the verb “standeth” is a perfect tense: it has stood and continues to stand. False teachers may topple some individuals, but they cannot overturn God’s work.

The foundation bears “this seal.” In the ancient world a seal marked ownership and authenticity; inscriptions were also carved on foundation stones to declare a building’s owner and purpose. Here the inscription has two parts, both drawn from Scripture.

The first reads, “The Lord knoweth them that are his.” These are the words of Moses during the rebellion of Korah (Numbers 16:5), when leaders within Israel challenged God’s appointed order. God then made plain who belonged to him and who did not. The parallel with Ephesus is striking: rebellion was arising from within the congregation. God’s knowledge of his own is personal and certain. He is not confused by appearances, and those who are truly his are held by him. This brings assurance to the faithful and humility to all who might presume to judge others’ hearts.

The second reads, “Let every one that nameth the name of Christ depart from iniquity.” It summarizes Moses’ command to separate from the tents of the rebels (Numbers 16:26), with echoes of the prophets’ call to depart and touch no unclean thing. To name the name of the Lord is to call on him and confess him. Such confession has a moral consequence: those who belong to the Lord turn away from wickedness, both the error that contradicts truth and the conduct that error produces. God’s seal rests on those who are being made holy.

The two lines belong together. God’s choosing and knowing come first, and human obedience follows as its evidence. Assurance and holiness are not rivals. Those whom the Lord knows show it by departing from iniquity, and in a time of confusion that combination marks the true people of God.

wordNotes.term: ὁ στερεὸς θεμέλιος τοῦ θεοῦ (ho stereos themelios tou theou) — the foundation of God … sure
wordNotes.explanation: Themelios is a foundation, and stereos means solid or firm. Paul uses foundation imagery for the church built on Christ and the apostolic message. Its firmness rests on God as builder and owner.

A seal authenticated a document or object and marked ownership. Here it functions like an inscription on a foundation stone. In Scripture God’s seal marks those who belong to him, as in Ezekiel’s vision and in Revelation.

verses.bibleText: But in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and of silver, but also of wood and of earth; and some to honour, and some to dishonour.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul extends the building image from the foundation to the household inside it. “In a great house” a visitor would find many kinds of containers. Some were “of gold and of silver,” costly pieces brought out for honored guests and special occasions. Others were “of wood and of earth,” common bowls, jars, and pots of baked clay used for kitchen work, storage, or the disposal of refuse, and thrown out when cracked or soiled.

The great house is the visible church, the household of God in its broadest form. Paul has just mentioned teachers within that household who have swerved from the truth. The professing community contains people who honor the Master and people whose conduct brings him dishonor. Jesus taught something similar when he spoke of wheat and tares growing together in one field and of a net that gathers good and bad fish until the sorting at the end of the age. The presence of unworthy members should not shock Timothy or shake his faith in God’s foundation.

The contrast “some to honour, and some to dishonour” concerns the use and destiny of the vessels. In Romans 9 Paul uses the same pair of phrases for the potter who makes vessels for different purposes. Here, though, the emphasis falls less on the material a vessel is made of and more on its condition and the use to which it is put. A dishonorable vessel is one unfit for the master’s table, and in the end such vessels are set aside.

The illustration is not fatalistic. The next verse shows that a person can be cleansed and become a vessel for honor. Paul’s purpose is to explain the mixed state of the church while calling each member to examine which kind of vessel he is becoming. The day of judgment will reveal the difference, but the choice of cleansing is offered now.

wordNotes.explanation: A general word for containers, utensils, or implements used in a household. Scripture often applies it to people as instruments in God’s hand, as when Paul is called a chosen vessel to carry Christ’s name.

wordNotes.term: εἰς τιμήν … εἰς ἀτιμίαν (eis timēn … eis atimian) — to honour … to dishonour
wordNotes.explanation: These phrases describe the purpose for which a vessel is used: honorable service or menial, dishonorable use. Applied to people, they distinguish those whose lives honor the Master from those whose conduct disgraces his house.

verses.bibleText: If a man therefore purge himself from these, he shall be a vessel unto honour, sanctified, and meet for the master's use, and prepared unto every good work.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“If a man therefore purge himself from these” draws the practical conclusion. The indefinite “a man” means anyone, so the invitation stands open to every member of the household. The verb means to clean out thoroughly. Paul used it at Corinth when urging the church to purge out the old leaven. “From these” most naturally refers to the dishonorable vessels just described, the false teachers and the corrupting influence of their words and ways. A believer must separate from their errors and refuse the fellowship that would defile him.

The result is a vessel “unto honour,” described in three ways. It is “sanctified,” set apart and made holy for God’s use, a perfect participle showing a settled condition. It is “meet for the master’s use,” serviceable to the owner of the house, who is the Lord himself. Paul uses the same adjective later of Mark, who had once failed but became useful for ministry (4:11), and of Onesimus, the runaway transformed by the gospel. Usefulness to God is not reserved for those with spotless pasts. And it is “prepared unto every good work,” standing ready for whatever service the Master requires.

An earthen pot cannot change its own material, but a person can be changed. Through repentance and the cleansing that Christ provides, someone once fit only for menial use can become precious to God. Holiness is God’s work in us, yet the verse also calls for a decisive personal response: turning from what defiles. The aim is readiness. A vessel kept clean is available whenever the Master reaches for it.

wordNotes.explanation: The compound verb means to cleanse out completely. Its only other New Testament use concerns removing the old leaven at Corinth, suggesting thorough separation from what corrupts, both in belief and in association.

wordNotes.term: εὔχρηστον τῷ δεσπότῃ (euchrēston tō despotē) — meet for the master’s use
wordNotes.explanation: Euchrēstos means useful or serviceable, and despotēs is the master of the household. Paul applies the adjective to Mark and to Onesimus, both of whom became useful after earlier failure.

verses.bibleText: Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace, with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul now describes what cleansing looks like in Timothy’s own life. “Flee also youthful lusts.” The command to flee appears repeatedly in Paul, always with a specific danger in view: flee fornication, flee idolatry, flee the love of money. Some temptations are not to be debated or managed; they are to be escaped.

“Youthful lusts” certainly includes sensual desire, which every young man must guard against, and a life of purity, temperance, and self-control is part of being a clean vessel. But the phrase reaches further. Timothy was probably in his thirties, still young compared with Paul and the elders he led. The desires that often accompany youth include impatience, self-assertion, ambition, love of argument, and attraction to whatever is new and fashionable. The verses that follow, with their warnings against quarrels and calls to gentleness, suggest that these temperamental temptations were much on Paul’s mind.

Fleeing is only half the command. Timothy must also “follow” four qualities, using a verb that means to pursue eagerly, to chase after. “Righteousness” is right conduct shaped by God’s will. “Faith” is trust in God and reliance on Christ. “Charity,” the KJV’s word for love, is self-giving care for God and others. “Peace” is harmony and wholeness in relationships. The first three appear in the parallel charge of 1 Timothy 6:11. The negative and positive belong together; an emptied heart left vacant soon fills again with what was driven out.

Timothy is to pursue these “with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart.” To call on the Lord is to worship and confess him. Those who do so from a pure heart are believers whose confession is matched by inward cleansing. Holiness is not pursued in isolation. Timothy needs companions of sincere devotion, and peace in particular is to be sought with them. The church’s fellowship of the pure in heart is itself a means by which God keeps his servants steady.

wordNotes.explanation: Epithymia means strong desire, usually disordered desire in this setting. Neōterikos, found only here in the New Testament, means characteristic of youth. The phrase covers passions typical of younger years, including sensuality, rashness, contentiousness, and the craving for novelty.

The verb can mean to persecute or, as here, to pursue zealously. Paul uses it for the earnest pursuit of virtues such as love, peace, and good, describing a life energetically directed toward what pleases God.

verses.bibleText: But foolish and unlearned questions avoid, knowing that they do gender strifes.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul returns once more to the danger of controversy. “Foolish and unlearned questions avoid.” The word for questions refers here to speculative debates, the kind of disputes the false teachers loved. They are “foolish,” lacking wisdom and morally culpable, and “unlearned,” the work of minds untrained in the truth and undisciplined in thought. Elsewhere Paul describes such teachers as understanding neither what they say nor the things they affirm so confidently.

The verb “avoid” means to refuse or have nothing to do with. Timothy is not to be drawn into these discussions, however interesting they appear. The reason is their fruit: “knowing that they do gender strifes.” The verb means to beget or give birth to. Speculative arguments give birth to quarrels, and quarrels divide congregations, wound relationships, and distract from the work of the gospel. A wise minister recognizes which conversations will bear that offspring and declines them before they begin.

wordNotes.explanation: Zētēsis can mean inquiry or debate; here the adjectives make it negative. Apaideutos means uninstructed or undisciplined. The phrase describes speculation by people who lack training in God’s truth and therefore generate confusion.
Literally “they beget fights.” Machē refers to conflict and quarreling of a nonphysical kind. Paul and James both trace such fighting to disordered desires and empty disputes.

verses.bibleText: And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Over against quarrels Paul sets a portrait of “the servant of the Lord.” The word is literally slave, a title Paul gladly applies to himself and his co-workers. A slave’s conduct is determined by his master. Because Timothy belongs to Christ, his manner as well as his message must reflect Christ. The phrase may also recall the Servant of the Lord in Isaiah, who would not strive or cry out, nor break a bruised reed.

The Lord’s servant “must not strive.” The word is the verb form of the quarrels just mentioned. A minister who is quarrelsome contradicts his calling, however orthodox his views. Instead, he must be “gentle unto all men,” kind and approachable toward everyone, believers and unbelievers, friends and opponents alike. The same word appears in some manuscripts of 1 Thessalonians 2:7, where Paul describes his gentleness among converts as a nursing mother cherishing her children.

He must also be “apt to teach,” the same qualification required of overseers in 1 Timothy 3:2. Gentleness does not replace instruction; it carries it. The servant must be able to explain the truth clearly, even to those who resist it.

Finally, he must be “patient,” a word that describes forbearance under wrong. It means bearing ill treatment without resentment or retaliation. Opposition is guaranteed for anyone who teaches truth amid error. The Lord’s servant absorbs hostility as his Master did, who when reviled did not revile in return.

wordNotes.term: δοῦλον κυρίου (doulon kyriou) — the servant of the Lord
wordNotes.explanation: Doulos means slave, one wholly at the disposal of a master. Paul uses it of himself and his fellow workers. Applied to a church leader, it stresses that the Lord determines both the content and the manner of his service.
Found only here in the New Testament, the adjective describes one who endures evil or wrong without resentment. It names patient forbearance toward opponents, a quality Christ displayed under abuse.

verses.bibleText: In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves; if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The servant’s qualities now take concrete form in his dealings with opponents. He works “in meekness instructing those that oppose themselves.” Meekness is gentleness joined with strength, the humble considerateness that refuses harshness, sarcasm, and brusque contempt. Jesus described himself as meek and lowly in heart, and he blessed the meek. The same quality Paul requires when restoring someone overtaken in a fault must mark the correction of those who resist the truth.

“Instructing” translates a verb that combines teaching and discipline. The opponents need correction of their errors and positive teaching of the truth. “Those that oppose themselves” describes people who have set themselves against the Lord’s servants and their message, whether as false teachers or as those they have influenced. Paul does not write them off. Even Hymenaeus had been disciplined with the hope that he would learn. The aim of correction is always restoration, never mere victory in argument.

The goal is stated with humility: “if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth.” Repentance is God’s gift. Scripture speaks of God granting repentance to Israel and to the Gentiles, and of his kindness leading people to it. The servant can teach, plead, and model the truth, but only God can change a heart. “Peradventure,” meaning perhaps, recognizes that the outcome rests with God and with the response of those he addresses. The servant cannot guarantee success. He is called to faithfulness and left to hope.

The repentance in view leads “to the acknowledging of the truth,” a phrase the Pastoral Letters use for coming to know and embrace the gospel. God wills all people to come to that knowledge. Repentance is a change of mind that issues in a changed direction; here it means turning from error to the truth, and from opposition to submission to Christ.

This verse corrects two opposite failures. Some defenders of truth become harsh and contentious, forgetting that their opponents are captives to be freed. Others grow so gentle that they no longer correct anything. Paul holds both together: firm instruction in a meek spirit, carried out in dependence on God.

wordNotes.explanation: Praÿtēs describes gentleness, humility, and courtesy, the opposite of roughness or sudden anger. It is a fruit of the Spirit and the spirit in which believers are to restore the erring and answer those who question their hope.

wordNotes.term: δώῃ αὐτοῖς ὁ θεὸς μετάνοιαν (dōē autois ho theos metanoian) — God … will give them repentance
wordNotes.explanation: Metanoia is a change of mind leading to a change of life. The verb “give” presents repentance as God’s gift, while the subjunctive expresses hopeful possibility, leaving the outcome with God.

verses.bibleText: And that they may recover themselves out of the snare of the devil, who are taken captive by him at his will.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The final verse looks behind human opposition to the spiritual power at work in it. Those who resist the truth are not merely stubborn thinkers; they are captives of the devil. The hope is “that they may recover themselves out of the snare of the devil.” The verb for “recover themselves” means to return to soberness, to come back to one’s senses after intoxication. Error had dulled their perception and distorted their judgment, much as strong drink does. Repentance brings them back to clear thinking about God and themselves.

The image then shifts to a hunter’s trap. The devil has set a “snare,” and these people have walked into it. Paul warned earlier that overseers must avoid the snare of the devil and that the desire for riches leads into a snare. False teaching is one of Satan’s most effective traps, because it captures the mind while appearing to enlarge it. In the great controversy between Christ and Satan, deception has always been the enemy’s chief weapon, from the garden onward.

They “are taken captive by him at his will.” The verb means to capture alive, the same verb Jesus used when he told Peter that he would catch men. The devil catches people alive and holds them for his purposes. Interpreters have debated the pronouns in the phrase. The KJV reads it most naturally: the captives are held by the devil to do his will. Some instead take the final words to mean that, once freed from the devil’s trap, they come to do God’s will. Either way the verse sets two masters before the reader and pictures release from one into the service of the other.

This understanding shapes how the Lord’s servant views opponents. They are prisoners to be rescued, not enemies to be crushed. That is why he must be gentle, patient, and dependent on God, for only God’s grace can break the trap. Christ came to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the gentle, truthful ministry of his servants is one way he still does it.

wordNotes.explanation: Found only here in the New Testament, the verb means to become sober again or regain one’s senses. It implies that error has worked like intoxication, clouding judgment until God grants clarity through repentance.
From a verb meaning to catch alive. Its only other New Testament use is Jesus’ promise that Peter would catch men. The perfect participle pictures captives taken and still held, awaiting release.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: What keeps a servant of Christ steady when friends desert, error spreads, and faithfulness brings hardship?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: Strengthened by Christ’s grace and anchored in his resurrection, the Lord’s servant endures hardship, handles the word of truth straight, pursues holiness, and seeks the restoration of those caught in error.
discussionQuestions: Why does Paul place the command to entrust the gospel to others beside the command to be strong in grace?
What do the soldier, the athlete, and the farmer each teach about faithful service?
How does the teaching that “the resurrection is past already” overthrow faith?
What does it mean in practice to handle the word of truth straight?
Why must correction of opponents be gentle, and what does God alone contribute?
commonMisunderstandings: Being strong in grace is not self-generated willpower; the strength is received continually from Christ.
“Rightly dividing” calls for straight, faithful handling of Scripture, not for cutting the Bible into isolated ages that cancel one another.
The resurrection hope is not a present spiritual experience only; the dead await a bodily rising at Christ’s return.
Gentleness toward opponents is not indifference to error; it is the manner by which truth is pressed for their restoration.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Hold together the gift and the demand: grace in Christ supplies the strength, while the minister must endure, study, flee, pursue, and teach with humility.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, and let his grace make you a faithful workman, a clean vessel, and a gentle servant who points others to the truth.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: The risen Christ unites believers to himself in death and life, promises a future bodily resurrection and reign, and remains faithful to his word.
flow: Jesus, the promised Son of David, died and was raised from the dead.
By faith and baptism a person dies with him to sin and begins to live with him.
Those who endure with Christ will share his reign when he returns and raises his people.
Denying Christ has grave consequences, yet his faithfulness remains for all who turn to him.
Today God grants repentance and opens the way out of the enemy’s snare.
simpleIllustrations: A soldier on active duty does not hire himself out for side work; loyalty to the commander shapes every choice.
Gangrene spreads steadily from a small wound, just as a small denial of the resurrection can unravel a person’s whole faith.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you die with Christ to sin, trust his faithfulness, and wait for the day he raises his people to reign with him?
cautions: Do not present endurance as earning salvation; it is faith continuing in Christ’s grace.
Do not make the warning of verse 12 a weapon against struggling believers; verse 13 sets Christ’s faithfulness beside it.
Do not imply that the dead are already enjoying the resurrection; Scripture places it at Christ’s appearing.

reflectionQuestions: Where am I trying to serve God by my own strength instead of drawing continually on the grace that is in Christ?
Whom am I helping to grow so that the gospel will be carried beyond my own life?
Which ordinary affairs have begun to entangle me so that pleasing my Lord is no longer my first concern?
Do I handle Scripture straight, or do I bend it toward the conclusions I already prefer?
When someone opposes the truth, do I respond with quarrelsome words or with patient, gentle correction?
